newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Low turnout in Ireland's referendum on bail laws.
newsitem.headline: Low turnout in Ireland's referendum on bail laws.

text.p: Ireland voted on Thursday in a referendum to decide whether to tighten its bail laws in an attempt to stem rising drug-related crime and in the wake of the suspected contract killing of crime reporter Veronica Guerin.

The country's coalition government called a poll to ask voters to approve a constitutional change which would allow courts to deny bail to people charged with a serious crime and who could commit more offences while awaiting trial.
But early estimates suggested that public concern about drugs and crime had not translated into enthusiasm for the poll.
With only a few hours of voting left, national broadcasting network RTE said the final turnout might be less that 40 percent -- the lowest referendum turnout in the Irish Republic's history.
In some counties less than 10 percent of the population voted. Commentators blamed bad weather and public confusion about the issues at stake.
Under the current system judges may deny bail only if they fear the suspect will not show up for trial or will try to interfere with witnesses or evidence.

The government called the referendum in June after public outrage when crime reporter Guerin was shot dead by hitmen in a suspected contract killing. Guerin made her name writing about gangland bosses and drug barons living and operating in Ireland.
Police believe one of them ordered her murder.
The price of heroin on the streets of Dublin has halved in recent years to around 10 Irish pounds ($17) a dose, or the equivalent of four pints of the nation's beloved stout beer.

Official statistics show that the number of crimes committed by people on bail has risen sharply from 2,613 in 1987 to 5,440 in 1995, and figures for this year were expected to show further increases.
The Irish Independent newspaper called on its readers to vote for a tightening of the law.
"Today we have an opportunity as members of the public to strike back at some of the criminals who have inflicted terror and suffering on us," it said in an editorial.
But lawyers and civil rights groups argue that the proposed change will mean that a suspect is guilty until proven innocent and jeopardise constitutional guarantees of freedom.
They fear the change will give police arbitrary power to recommend that suspects be denied bail and clog up the nation's already overburdened prisons.

Law and order has already become a campaign issue for a general election due in the next 12 months. The main opposition party, Fianna Fail, has plastered billboards with pictures of two hands grasping iron bars promising that criminals will be put "where they belong". ($=0.595 Irish Pounds)
